clue.text: German city providing meat (and food generally, upon reflection)

parts.note: ham is a cured meat

indicators.note: a reflection shows a thing back to front, so the word for food is read from right to left

parts.note: grub is slang for food in general

explanation.surface: A German city is praised for its meat and, on reflection, its food as a whole.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket looks like an aside about cuisine, but it holds wordplay: grub is informal British slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamburg is a major port city in northern Germany, so it is an example of a German city.

clue.text: Small house on top of Grasmoor's second ridge

parts.note: HO is the short form of house

indicators.note: the top of a down entry's word is its opening letter

parts.note: Grasmoor is a fell in the Lake District
the possessive ending supplies its letter
to second a proposal is to back it

explanation.surface: A tiny cottage sits on the summit of Grasmoor, a Lake District fell.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on top of' places one piece above the next.
explanation.definitionFit: A hogsback is a long steep-sided ridge shaped like a pig's back; the Hog's Back is one in Surrey.

clue.text: Film return of famous racehorse — extremely unpleasant

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the horse's name is read backwards

parts.note: Red Rum won the Grand National three times
foul means unpleasant, and most makes it extreme

explanation.surface: A famous racehorse makes a comeback in a thoroughly nasty way.
explanation.walkthrough: Red Rum is the Grand National winner of the 1970s, and its name backwards is a well-known palindrome trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Murder Most Foul is a 1964 Miss Marple movie, the title taken from Hamlet.

clue.text: American needing time for practice

parts.note: US for American
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: An American needs time to practise something.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage means customary practice, as in the established habits of a language or community.

clue.text: Travel with wife, pay half each

parts.note: to go is to travel
'my old Dutch' is Cockney slang for one's wife

explanation.surface: A couple on holiday agree to split the bills.
explanation.walkthrough: Dutch for wife comes from the Cockney phrase 'my old Dutch', short for duchess.
explanation.definitionFit: To go Dutch is an idiom meaning each person pays their own share of a bill.

clue.text: Stake needed, unlimited

indicators.note: without limits means the word loses its boundaries, the first and last letters

parts.note: what is needed is wanted

explanation.surface: A gambler is told a bet is required, with no upper limit.
explanation.walkthrough: WANTED with its outer W and D removed leaves ANTE.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker the ante is the stake each player puts into the pot before the deal.

clue.text: Unplaced horse, a length ahead of second roan racing

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: racing suggests letters dashing about and ending up in a new order

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for length
S is the abbreviation for second
taken as written

explanation.surface: A horse that failed to place was a length ahead of the roan that came second.
explanation.definitionFit: An also-ran is a horse that finishes outside the placings, and by extension any unsuccessful contender.

clue.text: More frugal once their rift is sorted out

indicators.note: sorting out means rearranging into a different order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A couple become more careful with money after settling their quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Thriftier is the comparative of thrifty, meaning careful and economical with money.

clue.text: Vandalised new gym, relevant in film

indicators.note: vandalised means smashed up, so the letters are broken apart and rebuilt

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A newly built gym that was trashed features in a movie.
explanation.definitionFit: Twelve Angry Men is the 1957 courtroom drama about a jury deliberating a murder case.

clue.text: Agile, agent crossing river

indicators.note: crossing here means going across and enclosing, so one word straddles the other

parts.note: a secret agent is a spy
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A nimble secret agent makes their way over a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Spry means lively and nimble, usually said of an older person, so it is a synonym of agile.

clue.text: Festoon of flowers for US actress and singer

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a wreath or chain of flowers
second meaning: Judy, star of The Wizard of Oz

explanation.surface: A floral tribute is laid out for an American star of stage and screen.
explanation.definitionFit: A garland is a decorative wreath of blossoms, and Judy Garland was the American actress-singer famous for Over the Rainbow.

clue.text: Mishandle wages at university

parts.note: screw is old British slang for wages or salary
a student in residence at university is said to be up

explanation.surface: Someone bungles the payment of salaries at a university.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are British usages: screw for pay, and being up at Oxford or Cambridge for attending university.
explanation.definitionFit: To screw up is an informal phrasal verb for botching or making a mess of something.

clue.text: Warder, no vegetarian?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a Yeoman Warder at the Tower of London
second meaning, taken literally: someone who eats beef

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful literal reading of the nickname for a Tower of London guard.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeoman Warders guarding the Tower of London are popularly called by this nickname, which read literally describes a meat eater.

clue.text: Sort of insurance policy quite needed by school?

parts.note: quite in the sense of completely
a British state secondary school taking pupils of all abilities

explanation.surface: A school is said to need a particular kind of insurance cover.
explanation.walkthrough: A comprehensive is a British state secondary school that does not select pupils by ability.
explanation.definitionFit: Fully comprehensive is the British term for motor insurance covering damage to your own vehicle as well as others.

clue.text: See 12
Disgusting rioting

definitions.meaning: second meaning: rising up in rebellion

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a condemnation of unrest; the two words are separate senses of one participle.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both nauseating and taking part in a revolt against authority.

clue.text: I don't know what a customs officer may do

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an informal shrug of ignorance

definitions.text: what a customs officer may do
definitions.meaning: second meaning, taken literally: frisk a traveller

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is the phrase taken literally, as an officer at a border might pat you down.
explanation.definitionFit: Search me is a colloquial expression meaning I have no idea, and literally describes a body search at the border.

clue.text: Rare eagle on silver tree

indicators.note: rare can mean undercooked or unusual, here suggesting the letters are in an unusual order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An uncommon bird perches on something made of silver.
explanation.definitionFit: The Seville orange is a bitter citrus tree grown in Spain, its fruit prized for marmalade.

clue.text: Beatles record — odd title, extremely bizarre

indicators.note: odd means strange or out of place, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: the two ends of this word

explanation.surface: A Beatles album is said to have a strange and very weird name.
explanation.definitionFit: Let It Be was the Beatles' final studio album and a hit single from 1970.

clue.text: What map line may show just short of lake and hill

indicators.note: short of means lacking, so the following item is taken away

parts.note: just in the sense of fair and even-handed
L is the abbreviation for lake
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A map line is said to stop just before a lake and a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just short of' reads as 'nearly reaching'; instead 'just' is the word and 'short of lake' drops its L.
explanation.definitionFit: The equator is the imaginary circle round the Earth's middle, drawn as a line on world maps.

clue.text: Very bad, if legal, squandering capital

indicators.note: squandering means throwing away, and the capital is the word's opening letter

parts.note: something legal is permitted by law

explanation.surface: Wasting money is deplorable even when it is within the law.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital looks like money in the surface; it means the first letter, so LAWFUL loses its L.
explanation.definitionFit: Awful is a straightforward synonym for terrible or of very poor quality.

clue.text: Singer — all things considered, get her off!

indicators.note: taking something off removes it, here two named words

parts.note: altogether means on the whole
taken as written, to be removed
taken as written, to be removed

explanation.surface: Taking everything into account, someone wants a singer removed from the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get her off!' sounds like a heckle, but GET and HER are removed from ALTOGETHER.
explanation.definitionFit: An alto is a singer with a low female or high male voice, so a type of singer.

clue.text: Jupiter, say, the king sheltering below

indicators.note: to shelter something is to hold it inside, so the first pair of words goes around the last

parts.note: taken as written
R for rex, Latin for king
below means underneath

explanation.surface: The king of the Roman gods keeps someone safe beneath him.
explanation.walkthrough: R stands for rex, Latin for king, a crossword convention; 'sheltering' puts the word for below inside the first two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Jupiter, wielder of lightning bolts, was known as the Thunderer; 'say' marks him as one example.

clue.text: Current doctor, fit for a change!

parts.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor

indicators.note: a change means the letters are altered into a different order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A present-day doctor is healthy, which makes a nice change.
explanation.walkthrough: Current looks like an adjective meaning present; it is the noun for a flow.
explanation.definitionFit: A drift is a slow current, such as the movement of water in an ocean.

clue.text: Tutor is itinerant holidaymaker

indicators.note: an itinerant travels from place to place, so these letters wander out of order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A travelling teacher is someone on holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: A tourist is a person travelling for pleasure, in other words on a holiday trip.

clue.text: Crow put him right off

indicators.note: off suggests something gone bad or disordered, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A crow appears to have scared someone away.
explanation.walkthrough: Crow looks like the bird; it is the verb meaning to gloat.
explanation.definitionFit: To crow is to boast exultantly, which is to triumph over a beaten rival.

clue.text: Monster consequently returned

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: ergo is Latin for therefore

explanation.surface: A monster came back as a result.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a man-eating giant of folklore, so a kind of monster.

clue.text: Train staff

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a train of followers attending a dignitary
second meaning: the attendants or personnel in someone's service

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it looks like railway employees; the two words are separate senses of one noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is a group of attendants accompanying an important person, which is both a train and a staff.
